pages.head: The Story
pages.html:
SNOWBOUND

The $89 Shovel

Fort Ashby, Mineral County, West Virginia. Friday, December 11, 1992.

The storm came in overnight and left a foot and a half of snow on the neighborhood. School is closed. The Mineral County Courier says the whole county is snowbound.

You have a shovel, a coffee can, and a plan. Over at LaVale Mall, in the window of Bits & Bytes Software, sits a pink box: GAME-MAKER, the kit that lets you design your own worlds, monsters and music without programming. It costs $89. In January it goes up to $129. Just down the hall is Bleeps, the arcade, where you spend every Saturday you can.

So this morning you hung out your sign at home, on the corner of Gale Street and Dunn Drive: Moten Snow-to-Software Operations, founder and operator. One dollar a scoop. Every driveway is a pixel of the game you are going to make.

Dig out your street, sled down Jamie Street, work Bowden Drive, and get to the mall before closing time. The box is yours.

pages.head: Getting Started
pages.html:
Getting Started

Type SNOWBND and press Enter. You need a VGA display. A Sound Blaster plays the music and the digitized sound effects; without one, the PC speaker beeps along.

From the menu, pick Play. Leave the menu alone for half a minute to watch a demonstration. Read Storyline shows the morning paper; Read Instructions is a short version of this manual.

The coffee can

There is no money counter on the screen - real shovelers don't have one either. Press F2 any time to tip out the coffee can and count it: the status screen shows your dollars, warmth and lives. You need $89 when you reach the register.

Warmth and lives

You start with 100 points of warmth and three lives. Plows, cars, carts, snowballs, a playful dog and the town bully all wear you down; hot cocoa warms you back up. If you get too cold you go home, warm up, and start that street over - with every dollar you've earned still in the can.

pages.head: Controls
pages.html:
Controls

↑ ↓ ← →
or W S A D		Walk. Walk into deep snow to shovel it.
Q E
keypad 7 9 1 3		Walk diagonally: Q up-left, E up-right; the number pad corners go all four ways. Holding two arrows at once won't do it - use these.
SpaceThrow a snowball the way you last walked.
EnterPick up what lies at your feet.
F1Help
F2Count the coffee can (money, warmth, lives)
F3 / F4Music on/off, sound effects on/off
F5 / F6Save / load a game
EscQuit to the menu

On the sled

← → or A DLean and steer. The sled drifts - steering builds up sideways speed.
↑ or WDig in your heels to slow down (hold it and you'll creep back uphill).
↓ or SPush off - one shove each time you press it. Tap it to get going again after a crash.
Q EBrake and steer left or right at the same time.

A joystick works too: directions walk or steer, either button throws.

pages.head: Shoveling
pages.html:
Shoveling for Dollars

Plain yard snow is just snow. The big, puffy deep snow heaped on driveways and front walks is work - and work pays. Walk into a heap and you scoop it: $1 a scoop, and the pavement underneath is clear.

Don't forget the front walks

Every neighbor wants the front walk cleared too - to reach the car, fetch the paper off the door mat, and keep Grandma from slipping on the steps. That's more scoops - and more dollars - at every house.

Things worth picking up

  • Dollar bills - $1. They blow all over the Jamie Street hill and the frozen creek.
  • A tip envelope - $5, left on a porch by a happy customer.
  • Hot cocoa - warms you up by 35. Outside Bleeps it's root beer instead: the snack bar sells nothing else.
  • Plow banks - the dirty heaps the plows leave along the road. Scoop one to pack more snowballs.

Snow forts

Kids behind snow forts lob a snowball every few seconds. Walk right into a fort to knock it flat (100 points) and it stops throwing - then shovel the pile it leaves for $2.

pages.head: Hazards
pages.html:
Who's Out in the Snow

SnowplowsThe state crews never stop. A plow fills a whole lane; cross the road behind it, never in front.
CarsThe far lane of Bowden Drive is busy when everybody comes home from work.
SnowballsFrom the forts. They home in on you, but they're slower than you are and melt after a couple of seconds. Your own snowballs knock them out of the air.
BiscuitThe friendliest dog in Fort Ashby. When you get close he runs straight at you, knocks you flat, and bounds off happy.
Big PeteThe bully. He follows you around, gives you one good shove, and strolls off pleased with himself - then comes looking again a few seconds later. A snowball gets him first: he strolls off without the shove.
Fire hydrantsBuried up to the cap. You can't shovel through one - walk around.
Shopping cartsLoose in the mall lot, rolling wherever the wind takes them.
IceSlides you the way its arrows point. The creek along Bowden Drive runs east and will carry you along if you cross on the ice instead of the bridge.

pages.head: The Six Streets and the Mall
pages.html:
From Sunrise to Closing Time

1. Gale Street - 7:00 AM

Your own street, pink with morning. Home is at Gale Street and Dunn Drive - Dad already dug out ours. Three neighbors along Gale and two more up Leota Street need their driveways and front walks dug out - about $49 with the tip. You are subbing on the News-Tribune route this morning, too: grab the bundle by the porch at home and leave a paper on each customer's door mat for 250 points. One plow works Gale, Biscuit is loose in the park, and a practice fort waits behind the fence. When you're done, head east to Leon Drive.

2. Jamie Street - Noon

Leon Drive brings you to the top of Jamie Street, closed for sledding: the longest run in town. The hill bends to the right all the way down, past three stands of trees: snowy firs and red and blue gates at the top, white birches in the middle, and the lamps of lower Jamie Street at the bottom, where somebody has strung Christmas lights on the firs. Boards in the trees on both sides count down from 9 to 1 as you go. The snow is banked up along the edges and nudges you back toward the middle, and where the run squeezes between trees, ripples in the snow point the way round and carry you with them. Steer around the rocks and trees, slow down on the moguls, and grab the dollars blowing down the run. Kids on toboggans cut across without looking. Past the last board there is one more steep drop between the lit firs, and then the checkered finish, with the street lamps of Bowden Drive lit just below it, drops you at the corner of Jamie and Bowden.

3. Bowden Drive - 4:30 PM

A long row of houses, everybody home from work - and most of them got the shovel out themselves. Two north-side neighbors still want a clear path from the car to the door, and two more wait across the frozen creek, down the paths through the pines. Take the footbridge over (the ice carries you east), and watch for Big Pete, who hangs around it. Two plows and a car share the road. The sign at the east end points the way to LaVale.

4. LaVale Mall - 8:00 PM

Night, lamps, and a parking lot full of buried cars of every color, in three rows with a lamp island in the middle of each. Lost? A lit sign at the far right edge of the lot points back to the mall. Every twenty seconds or so a squall blows through and the lot fills back in - shovel it again and the money keeps coming. Meltwater has frozen along the back of the lot into an icy lane that slides you east toward the stores. You'll need the lot: the streets alone rarely add up to $89, so count on the lot for the last $15 or $20, with the plows on the fire lane, the carts loose and Big Pete about. Bleeps, the arcade, is near the middle of the mall: every push on its door costs $1 for a game, worth 100 points and a little warmth. Bits & Bytes is at the right end. The register only opens with $89 in your can. Out front, a History Fair table has a Liberty Bell - push it to ring it for 1776 points.

pages.head: Tips
pages.html:
Tips from the Founder

  • Shovel up a driveway, not across it: you clear one column per trip.
  • Check F2 before you leave a street. Whatever you're short, the LaVale Mall lot makes up - and every dollar from the streets is one less scoop in the dark.
  • Throw a snowball at a homing snowball - yours always wins.
  • The plow banks along every road are free ammunition. Keep your pockets full before you walk into the park.
  • On the sled, brake before the tree islands, not in them. If you stop dead, push off with ↓.
  • Jamie Street bends right. Lean right now and then to stay in the middle, and let the banked snow and the ripples carry you round the squeezes.
  • When the mall lot starts to dust over, get in the open: the heavier the squall, the more scoops within reach.
  • If you go home cold, the street starts over with fresh snow - and fresh money. Your coffee can stays full.
  • Bleeps is tempting. Play all you want - the lot keeps snowing - but count the can before you head for the register.

pages.head: Credits
pages.html:
Credits

Design, pixels, levels, music and sound: Claude

Every block, monster, character, song and sound effect in SNOWBOUND was built as a genuine Game-Maker 2.0 file: four levels, 135 background blocks, 30 monster pictures, 23 kinds of monster, two characters drawn in 20 poses, nine Sound Blaster songs, fourteen digitized sounds and an Autodesk Animator FLI intro.

Made with GAME-MAKER by Recreational Software Designs.

For the founder and operator of Moten Snow-to-Software Operations, Fort Ashby, winter of 1992, who shoveled his way to a copy of Game-Maker at LaVale Mall - one driveway, one pixel at a time. See you at Bleeps.

items.title: Snowbound Hint Book
items.note: Answers hidden: use the red film
items.intro: From the founder's own notebook. Lay the red film over an answer to read it.

hints.q: How do I know how much money I have?
hints.a: Press F2 to tip out the coffee can: the status screen shows your Money.

hints.q: I got to the register without $89.
hints.a: Go back out to the mall lot. A squall blows through every twenty seconds or so and buries it again: more scoops, more dollars. The streets alone rarely add up to $89.
A $5 envelope beside Mrs. Haines' porch on Gale Street.

hints.q: What are the door mats on Gale Street for?
hints.a: The morning paper. Grab the bundle by the porch at home, dig out each walk, and step on the mat: 250 points a paper.

hints.q: What is a snow fort worth?
hints.a: Walk into it to knock it flat for 100 points, then shovel the pile it leaves for $2.

hints.q: How do I leave Gale Street?
hints.a: Head east to Leon Drive at the end of the street; it leads north to the top of Jamie Street.

hints.q: I keep crashing on the sled.
hints.a: Brake with Up before the tree islands, not in them. If you stop dead, push off with Down. The run bends right, so lean right now and then to keep to the middle, and let the ripples in the snow carry you round the squeezes.

hints.q: How long is the Jamie Street sled run?
hints.a: Three stands of trees: firs, birches, then the lamps and lit firs of lower Jamie Street. The boards in the trees count down from 9 to 1. After the 1 comes a last steep drop between the lit firs, then the finish line above Bowden Drive.

hints.q: The creek ice carries me away.
hints.a: It runs east. Cross on the bridge instead of the ice.

hints.q: Big Pete won't stop shoving me.
hints.a: He shoves once, strolls off and comes back a few seconds later. A snowball sends him off before he can shove. Scoop a plow bank for more snowballs.

hints.q: What does the bell at the mall do?
hints.a: Push it. It rings for 1776 points, once, and swings the rest of the night.
Throw one of your own at them: yours always wins.
Grab hot cocoa, or the root beer outside Bleeps (35 warmth each). If you go home cold, the street starts over with fresh snow, and your coffee can stays full.

hints.q: Some say the felt-maker left something behind...
hints.a: The snowman behind your house lost a mitten. Where a mitten drops, a trail starts.

hints.q: I found the mitten. Now what?
hints.a: The pine right behind it is only painted on. Walk straight through it and follow the trail into the woods. What you can't push, stoop for with Enter.

In the park across Gale Street, find your snowman at the bottom of the park and the red mitten just below it. Walk down into the pines there: the trail runs down, right and down again to a hollow. Press Enter on the felt egg to pick it up, then push the frozen toboggan for a ride to Jamie Street.

items.title: The Mineral Courier
items.headline: AREA SNOWBOUND
items.deck: Foot and a half overnight in Mineral County; schools closed; plows out on every road

photo.caption: Gale Street at dawn: one driveway done, the rest waiting.

columns:
FORT ASHBY - A storm that came in overnight left a foot and a half of snow across Mineral County, closing schools and sending state plow crews out on every road before dawn.

Residents of Gale Street, Dunn Drive and Leota Street woke to find cars buried to the mirrors.

Neighbors want front walks cleared as well as driveways. "Grandma's coming at noon and my steps are a skating rink," one Leota Street resident said. "Somebody is going to make a fortune today."

Jamie Street is closed to traffic and open to sleds.

Over the line in LaVale, Maryland, stores plan to open on time. The Bleeps arcade promises the heat will be on.

A local software shop reports one copy of a popular game-making kit left in the window at $89. The price goes up in January.
briefs: A sign has gone up at Gale and Dunn: one dollar a scoop, founder and operator on duty.
The fire department asks residents to dig out hydrants near their homes.
Clearing by noon. Squalls near the mall after dark.

entries.html: Papers out (subbing on the route again). Sign is up. Coffee can is empty. Goal: $89 before the mall closes.
Gale Street done. Mrs. Haines tipped $5! Leota next.
Jamie Street is closed for sledding. Fastest way to Bowden. Lost my hat on the moguls.
Bowden Drive. Big Pete again. Snowball solved it.
LaVale lot keeps filling back in. Good. Count: almost there. DO NOT spend it all at Bleeps.

items.title: Thank-you letter
items.body:
Thank you for registering SNOWBOUND. You helped a kid with a shovel buy a pink box, and that pink box made this game.

As promised, your printed map of Fort Ashby is in this box, along with the hint book and a few things from the founder's coffee can.

SNOWBOUND II: Spring Thaw is next: mud season, a lawn mower, and a used 486 at the flea market. Watch The Sandbox Scoop and the BBS for news.

We promise to keep making games.

news.head: Snowbound: how Sandbox Software began
news.html: Hello, and welcome to the very first Sandbox Scoop. Fort Ashby, West Virginia, Friday, December 11, 1992: a foot and a half of snow, no school, and a pink box in the window of Bits & Bytes Software at LaVale Mall: GAME-MAKER, $89 until January. Snowbound: The $89 Shovel is the true(ish) story of how this company was paid for, and our first game. Dig out the neighbors’ driveways at a dollar a scoop, deliver the papers, sled down Jamie Street and get to the register before closing time. Mind Biscuit. He is very friendly.

news.head: SNOWBOUND II: Spring Thaw
news.html: The snow is melting in Fort Ashby, and the founder has a new plan: mow lawns all through mud season. Registered SNOWBOUND players get it free when it’s done.

news.head: Around the Sandbox: A company started with a snow shovel
news.html: This company was paid for one driveway at a time. When the big storm closed school on December 11, the founder shoveled the neighborhood at a dollar a scoop until there was enough for a copy of GAME-MAKER. Christmas vacation did the rest. The office is a desk, the family 286 and a stack of graph paper. The shovel is in the corner, in case we ever need another program.

news.head: In the workshop: The future, as we see it
news.html: Everybody knows what the year 2000 will be like: flying cars, robots everywhere and dinner in a pill. Our next game goes there to find out. In In The Year 2000! a kid and his robot dog have until 3:00 to get a science report to the Fair. The robot dog is the problem.

news.head: Letters: The mailbag is empty
news.html: This is issue 1, so nobody has written to us yet. Be the first! Tell us how many dollars you scooped, which hill you sledded best, and whether Biscuit got you. The first letter we get goes right here.
